steps.text:
What the games say. In endgames that are close (neither side clearly winning) you make a big error on about 10.5% of moves. Your opponents, in the same games, about 8.8%. That gap is not the clock: it is the same after matching for time left. In endgames where you are already winning comfortably you are as good as they are or better.

So the work is on close endgames, and the cuts below say where in them.

Where the gap is widest.
  • You have a passed pawn: 12.5% against 9.3%. With the pawn on the fifth rank or further: 14.8% against 10.0%.
  • King moves and pawn moves are where the extra errors are. Rook moves are fine.
  • Rook endings: 9.2% against 7.3%. They are in about three of every ten of your endgames; rooks with minor pieces are in seven of ten.
  • Up a pawn or two: 9.7% against 7.2%.
A caution: about 45 different cuts were tried to get these, so treat them as a pointer for what to study, not as proven findings. You are one to two points worse on nearly every cut. The gap is broad, and these are the places it is widest or most frequent.

The order of the lessons.
  1. Support before pushing. A passed pawn goes forward with its king or rook, not ahead of them.
  2. King in front of the pawn. Opposition, key squares, and how to defend against it.
  3. The square of the pawn. Whether a king catches a running pawn, without counting.
  4. Rook endings: the winning position (Lucena), the drawing position (Philidor), and rooks behind passed pawns.
  5. Trading: pieces when ahead, pawns when behind. King to the centre when the queens come off.
The rule inside each lesson is standard teaching. The data only chose the order. Every position in these lessons with seven pieces or fewer has been checked move by move against an endgame tablebase, which is a complete solved table, so "wins" and "draws" here are facts and not engine opinions.

cards.t: Where your endgames leak, and the order to fix it

steps.text:
Push, or bring the king? White to move. The pawn is passed and nothing stops e4.

It is the wrong move. e4 draws. Ke4 wins.
After e4 the black king takes up its post in front of the pawn with Kd6. Your king can never get past it. This position is a draw, and the next lesson shows the defence in full.

After Ke4 the king leads and the pawn follows behind it. Black has to give way to one side, and the white king goes round the other.

The pawn does not move until the king has cleared its road. That is the whole idea, and it is the same idea in every ending with a passed pawn.
The same question with rooks on. White to move, a pawn up. e6 looks natural and throws the win away.
After e6 your king has lost its shelter: the square e6 was where it would have hidden from checks. Now the rook checks from behind for ever. Draw.
Ke6 instead. King first. The king keeps its shelter in front of the pawn, Ra8+ is in the air, and the pawn comes up behind the king later. This wins.

Before you push a passed pawn, three questions.
  1. Once it has moved, is it attacked more times than it is defended?
  2. Is the square in front of it one I control, or will a piece simply sit there and block it?
  3. Could the king or the rook step up first instead?
If in doubt, improve the helper and push next move. A passed pawn that waits one move is still a passed pawn.

Your own games agree with this. With a passed pawn on the board your extra errors are spread over every kind of move, and you push it exactly as often as your opponents do. So the problem is not too much pushing or too little. It is the order: pawn first, helpers second.

The deck Your passed pawns has positions from your own games to practise on.

One position, two results. King and pawn against king. If it is Black's move here, White wins. If it is White's move, it is a draw.

The reason is called the opposition: the kings face each other with one square between them, and whoever has to move must step aside and let the other king through.
Black to move has to give way. Ke7, and the white king goes round the other side with Kc6. This is outflanking.
Kd8 Kd6. Opposition again. Not the pawn yet: d5 here would let Black draw with Kc8.
Ke8 Kc7. The king now guards d6, d7 and d8, every square the pawn has to cross. Only now does the pawn run.
Back to the start, but with White to move. White has to give way instead. Whatever the king does, the black king stays in front, and pushing the pawn only walks into stalemate. Draw.

Key squares. You do not have to work out the opposition every time. For a pawn that has not crossed the middle of the board, the three squares two ranks in front of it are its key squares. Here: d5, e5 and f5 for the pawn on e3.

If your king reaches any one of them, the position is won, whoever is to move.
Ke4 takes the opposition. Kd6 Kf5: outflank, and the king is on a key square.
The pattern repeats all the way up the board. Opposition (Ke5), outflank (Kf6), and only then does the pawn step up behind the king.
King on the sixth rank in front of its pawn. This wins whoever is to move. Here Kd8 Kf7, and the pawn walks through e6, e7, e8.

The exception: rook's pawns. With an a-pawn or an h-pawn there is no outside to go round. If the defending king gets to the corner in front of the pawn, it is a draw however well your king stands.

So when you are trading down to a single pawn, a rook's pawn is the one to avoid being left with, and the one to leave your opponent with.

cards.t: King in front of the pawn

steps.text: You are Black, a pawn down, and the pawn has just come to the sixth rank. Your king has three squares to go back to. One of them draws.
Ke8. Straight back. From here you can answer whichever side the white king comes up.
Kd6 Kd8. Their king steps up beside the pawn and you face it. You have the opposition.
e7+ Ke8 Ke6. Stalemate. If White backs off instead, you do the same thing again. Draw.
The same position with the wrong retreat: Kd8 instead of straight back. Now Kd6 and it is White who has the opposition.

Ke8 e7 Kf7 Kd7, and the pawn queens.The defender's rule, in three parts: stay in front of the pawn. When you are pushed back, go straight back. When their king steps up beside the pawn, step in front of it.

cards.sub: straight back, then face the king

steps.text:
A pawn runs for the queening square and a king chases it. You do not need to count moves.

Draw a square with the pawn in one corner and the queening square in another. Here the pawn on b4 has four steps to go, so the square is b4, f4, f8, b8.

If the king is inside the square, or can step into it on its move, it catches the pawn. If not, the pawn queens.
Here the king on g5 is outside the square and it is White's move. The pawn simply runs, and the king stays one step short the whole way.
The same position with Black to move. Kf5 steps into the square.
Now the king keeps pace along the diagonal and arrives in time to take the pawn.

A pawn on its starting square can jump two squares, so draw the square as if the pawn already stood on the third rank. Here that is b3, g3, g8, b8. The king on h4 is outside it, so with White to move the pawn queens.

When to use it. Before you trade the last pieces into a pawn race, or let one pawn go to chase another, draw the square first.

One caution. The rule is for a lone pawn against a lone king. If the attacker's king can block the defender's path, or another pawn is in the way, count the moves instead.

Most rook endings with one extra pawn come down to two positions. This is the winning one.

Your pawn is on the seventh rank, your king is in front of it, and their king is cut off by your rook. One problem: your king is boxed in. If it steps out, their rook checks it straight back in.
Re1+ first. Push their king one file further away.
Re4. The key move: the rook goes to the fourth rank. It will be a shelter for your king, four ranks up the board. This is the bridge.
Black can only wait. Now the king steps out, and walks down the board towards the checking rook.

Rg4. The rook blocks the last check. The checks are over and the pawn queens.What to remember: pawn on the seventh with the king in front of it; rook to the fourth rank; king out and towards the rook; block.
This is the drawing one. You are Black and a pawn down. Your king stands on the queening square. The defence has two halves.
First half: rook to your third rank (the sixth, when you are Black). Rb6. It keeps their king from stepping forward. They can check, and your king just steps to e7 and back.
The only way for White to make progress is to push the pawn. e6. That push is your signal.
Second half: rook to the far end of the board. Rb1. Now that the pawn stands on e6, their king has lost the square where it would have hidden from checks.
Check from behind, for ever. The king has nowhere to hide. Draw.

What loses. The same ending with the rook sitting passively on the back rank. Kf6 and the king walks in, the pawn follows to e6 and e7, and the passive rook can do nothing about it. With a centre pawn, this is lost.

So: rook on the third rank until the pawn advances, then to the far end and check.
Behind your own pawn. Every step the pawn takes gives your rook more room, and their rook is stuck in front of it as a blocker. Here White wins by simply walking the king up to b7.
The king arrives, the blocking rook has to move away, and the pawn queens.

The same pawn and the same kings, with the rooks swapped. Now your rook is the one stuck in front, and theirs is behind the pawn. This is a draw.

Your rook cannot leave a8 without letting the pawn go. When your king comes up to free it, their rook checks from behind and there is nowhere to hide.

The same rule from the other side. When they have the passed pawn, your rook goes behind it. From there it attacks the pawn all the way up the board and keeps its freedom, and their rook ends up tied to defending.

In your close rook endings the extra errors are in king and pawn moves, and your rook moves are as good as your opponents'. So read this lesson as being about the pawn: before it advances, ask where its rook is.

Ahead: trade pieces. Behind: trade pawns.

The reason is that a piece cannot win by itself. King and knight against king is a draw. King and bishop against king is a draw. An extra piece wins only because it helps a pawn to queen. So the side that is ahead needs pawns left on the board, and the side that is behind wants them gone.
White is a whole knight up. It is Black's move, and Black draws on the spot.
h5. It offers to trade the last pair of pawns. After gxh5+ Kxh5 White has king and knight against a bare king, which cannot be won.
The same position with White to move. Kf4 stops the trade: now h5 is met by g5, keeping the pawn. White keeps the pawn, and the extra knight wins.

h5 g5. The pawn steps past and stays on the board. This is winning.

When you are ahead, every pawn trade deserves a second look. When you are behind, pawn trades are your friend, and the last pawn is the one to hunt.

King to the centre once the queens are off. In the middlegame the king hides. In the endgame it is a strong piece, and the pawn lessons show why: the result usually depends on which king gets in front of which pawn first.

In your endgames without queens your king stands slightly further from the centre than your opponents' kings do. The difference is small. But the first two or three moves after the queens come off are the cheapest moment to fix it: if nothing is hanging and there is nothing to take, the king move towards the centre is rarely wrong.

cards.t: What to trade, and where the king goes
